newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. withdraws invitation to Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. withdraws invitation to Belgrade.

text.p: The United States has withdrawn its invitation to the Serbian government to attend high-level talks in Geneva this week aimed at enhancing economic cooperation in southeast Europe, a U.S. official said on Tuesday.
Belgrade has been shaken by two weeks of street protests since the socialist government annulled an opposition victory in the capital and other cities in elections on November 17.

Nicholas Burns, a U.S. State Department spokesman, said on Monday that Washington would react with outrage against any use of force against anti-government protesters who Washington says are demonstrating peacefully over alleged vote-rigging.
The U.S. official in Geneva told Reuters that the decision was linked to Monday's State Department warnings.
Asked whether the U.S. invitation to Belgrade to participate in the multilateral talks had been officially withdrawn, the U.S. official told Reuters: "It has, yes."
"The U.S. charge d'affaires delivered the message this morning or last evening in Belgrade," he added.

"It (the decision) tracks closely with the statement by Nick Burns of December 2 that we will reserve the right to take any action necessary to express our displeasure at this fundamental refutation of democratic rights of the Serbian people."
France told Serbia on Tuesday it faced a severe warning from the international community if it cracked down on opposition.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux told reporters: "Authorities in Belgrade should expect a severe warning from the international community if they choose the path of direct confrontation." He added: "They must on the contrary look for an opening and dialogue."
The State Department also said it had sent a "very stiff message" to Belgrade that it should give up attempts to re-run municipal elections it lost last month.

In Belgrade on Tuesday, radio staff said that Serbian authorities had ordered Belgrade's only independent radio station B-92 shut down amid a wave of opposition street protests against President Slobodan Milosevic.
The original invitation to the three-day talks, opening in the Swiss city on Wednesday, was signed by President Clinton and mainly sent to foreign ministers.

Richard Schifter, special advisor to the President for National Security Affairs and Secretary of State for the Southeast European Cooperative Initiative, is chairing the meeting to be attended by foreign ministers and deputy foreign ministers from Europe.

Yves Berthelot, executive secretary of the U.N. Economoic Commission for Europe (ECE), is also to attend the meeting. The Geneva-based agency is the main U.N. body promoting economic cooperation betwen Europe and North America.

A White House statement issued on October 28 said the initiative was aimed at addressing the most urgent aspects of shared economic and environmental problems in the southeastern European region. This included attracting private capital to complement existing international funding.
